title: Flip Neighbour Signs for the Biggest Sum
statement:
You get an n × n integer grid matrix. One move picks two cells that share a side and multiplies both by -1. You may make any number of moves.

Return the largest possible sum of all cells.

examples.why: Flip the two -1s: first the top-right with the top-left (1 → -1, -1 → 1), then the top-left with the bottom-left. All four cells end positive.
Three negatives. Moves change the count of negatives by 0 or ±2, so one stays negative. Put that sign on the 1: 18 − 2 = 16.
Flip the -2 with the 0. A zero can soak up the spare minus sign for free.

hints: Try a few moves on paper. Can you move a minus sign from one cell to any other cell, not just a neighbour?
Flipping along a path moves a minus sign step by step, so any two minus signs can meet and cancel. What does a move do to the number of negative cells?

Every move changes the count of negatives by −2, 0 or +2, so its parity never changes. If the count is even, all can be positive. If odd, exactly one cell stays negative: make it the one with the smallest absolute value.

explain.intuition:
A single move between neighbours -a, b gives a, -b: the minus sign moved one step. Repeating along a path carries a minus sign anywhere in the grid, and when two minus signs meet in neighbouring cells, one move cancels both. So the only thing you cannot change is the parity of the number of negative values: each move flips two signs, changing the count by −2, 0 or +2.

If the count of negatives is even, every value can end non-negative: the answer is the sum of absolute values. If it is odd, one minus sign must survive, and you are free to park it on any cell. Park it on the cell with the smallest absolute value, which costs 2 · minAbs. A zero anywhere makes that cost 0, and zeros never need counting as negatives.
steps: Walk the grid. Add |v| to total, count the negatives, and track minAbs, the smallest |v|.
If the number of negatives is even, return total.
pitfalls: Leaving the leftover minus sign on one of the originally negative cells. In [[-4, 2, 2], [2, 2, 2], [2, 2, 2]] it belongs on a 2, giving 16, not 12.
Thinking only neighbouring negatives can cancel. Signs travel, so two far-apart negatives also cancel.
Subtracting minAbs once instead of twice. The cell goes from +minAbs to −minAbs.

solutions.title: Explore every reachable sign pattern
solutions.idea: A state is which cells are flipped. BFS over moves visits every reachable pattern; keep the best sum. Only feasible for tiny grids.

solutions.title: Parity of the negatives
solutions.idea: Signs can travel and cancel in pairs, so only the parity of the negative count matters. With an odd count, the smallest absolute value keeps the minus sign.

followups: Return an actual sequence of moves that reaches the best sum. How many moves can it take at most?
What if a move may only pair cells in the same row? Which parts of the argument still hold?
